---
<!-- dfn-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathbf{P}\subset \mathbb{R}^4$  be a compact convex polytope with non-empty interior, $y\in Int~\mathbf{P}$.
 A \textit{normal to the boundary of $\mathbf{P}$ emanating from }$y$ is a line $yz$ such that $z\in \partial \mathbf{P}$   such that  $yz$ is orthogonal to some support plane containing $z$.
<!-- end dfn-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{Thmmain}
  Each generic \footnote{The definition of genericity is given in Section \ref{SecGen}} simplex in $\mathbb{R}^4$ contains a point with at least $14$ emanating normals to the boundary.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A sphere is said to be inscribed in a convex polytope $\mathbf{P}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ if it is contained in $\mathbf{P}$, and the sphere is tangential to (at least) $n+1$ facets of $P$.

A spherical polytope is a polytope that fits in some open hemisphere. It is always assumed to be spherically convex. For a spherical polytope $P\subset S^n$, an inscribed sphere is defined in the same way.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $\Delta\subset S^3$ be a convex spherical tetrahedron. Let $O_{\Delta}$ be the center of the inscribed sphere. The polytope $\Delta$ is called \textit{perfect} if $O_{\Delta}\in Core(\Delta)$.

A vertex $V$ of a convex polytope $\mathbf{P}\subset \mathbb{R}^4$ is called \textit{perfect} if $Spher(V)$ is a perfect  spherical tetrahedron.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A spherical segment $AB\subset S^{n-1}$ is called \textit{short} if $|AB|<\pi/2$; otherwise, it is called \textit{long}.

A critical point of $SQD_y^{sph}$ is short (respectively, long) if the normal segment $yz$ is short (respectively, long).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemmaSaddle}
For a perfect spherical simplex, an edge $e$ contains a short critical point (which is automatically a saddle point) of $SQD^{sph}_{O_\Delta}$  iff $O_{\Delta}$ projects onto $e$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
There are two conditions for an edge to contain a saddle point: one is that $y$ projects onto $e$, and the other one
is that  angles between the plane $(ey)$ and the faces incident to $e$ are acute. This is true for the point $y=O_{\Delta}$ since the plane $(ey)$  bisects the angle at the edge $e$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemmaTriangTwoEdges}
Let $F=ABC$ be a spherical triangle, and let $X \in Core(F)$. Then $X$ projects onto at least two edges of $F$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assume the contrary. Then  the function $SQD^{sph}_X: \partial F\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ has exactly one short maximum attained, say, at the vertex $A$. The vertices $B$ and $C$ are not maxima. Then there exists an obtuse angle incident to the vertex $B$ and  an obtuse angle incident to the vertex  $C$,  see Fig. \ref{pic2cases}.

\textbf{Case 1, } Fig. \ref{pic2cases}. These two obtuse angles lie in different triangles  $AXB$, $BXC$, $CXA$. Then one of them (say, $AXB$) necessarily has an obtuse angle incident to $X$. The third angle in this triangle is acute. Finally $\angle AXB>\pi/2, \angle ABX > \pi/2, \angle BAX < \pi/2, |XA|<\pi/2$. Such a triangle does not exist.

\textbf{Case 2.} The obtuse angles are $XBC$ and $XCB$. Then we obtain local minima of $SQD_X^{sph}$ at $AB$ and $AC$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemmaInc}
If $\Delta$ is a perfect  spherical  tetrahedron, then the spherical squared distance function $SQD^{sph}_{O_\Delta}$ has at least $10$ short critical points.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The maxima of $SQD^{sph}_{O_\Delta}$ are attained at some vertices, and all maxima are short. Local minima are attained at some facets and saddle points at some edges, all of them are also short. Prove that $SQD^{sph}_{O_\Delta}$ has at least $4$ saddles which will immediately imply the desired statement. 

Since $O_{\Delta}$ is the center of the inscribed sphere, it projects to all the facets.

By Lemmata \ref{lemmaSaddle}, \ref{lemmaTriangTwoEdges}, each facet contributes at least two critical edges. Each edge  occurs twice, so
 $O_\Delta$ projects onto at least 4 edges of $\Delta$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{propInc}
Suppose that a generic convex polytope $\mathbf{P}\subset \mathbb{R}^4$ has at least one perfect vertex. Then $\mathbf{P}$ contains a point with at least $14$ emanating normals.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First remind that if a point $y\in \mathbf{P}$ lies very close to a vertex $V$, then the critical points of $SQD_y$ lying on the faces that are incident to $V$ (excluding the point $V$) are in bijection with short critical points of $SQD_y^{sph}$.



Next, we make use of a technique developed  in \cite{NasPan}, \cite{NasPan2}.

Pick the ray $VO_\Delta$, where $\Delta = Spher(V)$. Let the point $y$ keep moving along the ray with starting position $y = V$. Just after the start we have (at least) $12$ critical points of $SQD_y$: a local maximum at $V$,  at least $10$ critical points on the faces incident to $V$ (by Lemma \ref{lemmaInc}) and a global maximum. If there are more critical points, their total number is at least $14$.

The point $y$ keeps moving until the \textit{first event},  which is either a bifurcation of $SQD_y$,  or  the point $y$ leaves the
interior of $\mathbf{P}$. We have the following case analysis:




(a) The point $y$ leaves the polytope $\mathbf{P}$. This means that $y$ hits one
of the facets which is not incident to the vertex $V$. Right before this,
$y$, we have  an additional minimum attained at this facet. This minimum is not mentioned among $12$ <<old>> critical points. The <<old>> critical points persist since there was no bifurcation.

(b)The first event is a birth of two new critical points. This gives us $14$ normals.

(c) One of the <<old>> critical points dies. The pairwise distances between $11$  <<old>>  critical points (excluding the global maximum) keep increasing, so  they cannot collide. 
The only remaining case is if some 2-saddle $s$ meets the global maximum $V'$. Recall
that $s$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto one of the edges incident to $V$. Therefore, $V'$ is the endpoint of this edge. However, if $s$
meets $V'$ before $y$ leaves $\mathbf{P}$, then $|Vy|>|VV'|$, so $V'$ can't be a maximum of $SQD_y$ for the point $y=V$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
Let $O$ be the center of the inscribed sphere of a simplex $\mathbf{P}$. Then the maximum of $SQD_O$ is attained at a perfect vertex.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Indeed, let $V$ be this maximum and $\Delta = Spher(V)$. The points $O, O_{\Delta}, V$ are collinear, so $O_{\Delta} \in Core(\Delta)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
For $y \notin \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{P})$, we have:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Local maxima of $SQD_y$  are attained at some  vertices of $\mathbf{P}$.
  \item Local minima of $SQD_y$ are attained at some facets of $\mathbf{P}$.
  \item Saddles with Morse index $2$ of $SQD_y$ are attained at some  edges of $\mathbf{P}$.
   \item Saddles with Morse index $1$ of $SQD_y$ are attained at some  $2$-faces of $\mathbf{P}$.
   \item If $y$ crosses transversally one sheet of $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{P})$, a pair of critical points of  $SQD_{y}$ either dies or is born. This situation is called a bifurcation.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We call local maxima (local minima) just maxima and minima for short.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{DefGen} A polytope $\mathbf{P}$ with the vertex set $\mathbf{V}$ is generic if  affine hulls of any two subsets of
$\mathbf{V}$ are neither parallel nor orthogonal, unless this is dictated by unavoidable reasons. For example,
  \begin{description}
  \item[i] No two edges  are orthogonal.
  \item[ii]  No edge is parallel to a face, unless they are incident. 
                                                             
\end{description}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
